terms.d: A unit of length equal to one billionth of a meter.
terms.e: About 1/100,000 the width of a human hair. It's used in generation names like "5nm process," but it doesn't literally refer to an actual circuit dimension.
terms.u: When talking about process generation names, film thickness or line width

terms.d: A material that doesn't conduct electricity.
terms.e: It acts as a wall between wires or electrodes so they don't short out.
terms.u: Oxide films, interlayer dielectrics, gate dielectrics

terms.d: A different element mixed into a pure material.
terms.e: Added on purpose, it's doping; mixed in by accident, it causes defects.

terms.d: An atom or molecule that has become electrically charged by losing or gaining electrons.
terms.e: Because it's charged, an electric field can accelerate it or change its direction.

terms.d: A particle that carries electricity in a semiconductor — electrons and holes.
terms.e: Current is ultimately just carriers moving. The more carriers there are and the faster they move, the better current flows.
terms.u: Almost always, when explaining current, doping or mobility

terms.d: The empty spot left behind when an electron leaves; it moves like a positively charged particle.
terms.e: Picture an empty space in a parking lot shifting along as cars move into it.

terms.d: The width of the energy range electrons can't have.
terms.e: A wide gap means an insulator, a narrow one means close to a conductor, and semiconductors sit in between. Silicon's is about 1.1 eV.
terms.u: Classifying materials, leakage current, LEDs and solar cells

terms.d: The energy height that serves as the reference for how full of electrons the states are.
terms.e: Like the water level in a glass, it's the reference line showing how far up electrons are filled.
terms.u: Explaining PN junctions, MOS capacitors and threshold voltage

terms.d: Deliberately mixing a small amount of another element into a semiconductor to control how well it conducts.
terms.e: N-type adds electrons; p-type adds holes. It's a bit like adding a pinch of salt to change a dish's flavor.
terms.u: Forming source/drain and wells, ion implantation

terms.d: A structure joining p-type and n-type semiconductors that lets current flow easily in only one direction.
terms.e: Like a one-way door that lets current through in only one direction.
terms.u: Diodes, between a transistor's source/drain and the substrate

terms.d: How fast carriers move when an electric field is applied.
terms.e: Think of it as how well something runs when pushed with the same force.
terms.u: Transistor performance, boosters such as strained silicon

terms.d: The spontaneous spreading of atoms or molecules from high concentration to low.
terms.e: Like a drop of ink slowly spreading through water. It speeds up with heat, which is why impurities spread during annealing.
terms.u: Annealing after doping, what barrier metals block

terms.d: A thin round disc, usually sliced from silicon, that chips are built on.
terms.e: Like stamping many cookies from one sheet of dough, many chips are made at once on a single wafer.
terms.u: The starting point of every process; 300 mm diameter is mainstream today

terms.d: A solid whose atomic arrangement continues unbroken in one orientation.
terms.e: Think of a wall of bricks laid perfectly with no gaps or misalignment. When the crystal is off, electrical properties waver.

terms.d: A cylindrical single-crystal block made by melting and solidifying silicon.
terms.e: Slice this block thin and you get wafers — like cutting thin slices off a salami.
terms.u: The first step of wafer manufacturing

terms.d: A method of growing an ingot by dipping a seed crystal into molten silicon and slowly pulling it up while rotating.
terms.e: It resembles the experiment of growing crystals by dipping a string in a solution and slowly lifting it.

terms.d: Growing a thin single-crystal layer on a wafer surface in the same crystal orientation.
terms.e: It adds one more layer on top that's cleaner and better controlled than the wafer itself.
terms.u: Wafer manufacturing, forming FinFET and GAA channels

terms.d: A process that flattens a surface using chemicals and abrasives.
terms.e: A polishing step that smooths out a bumpy surface. It's essential before stacking a new layer on top.
terms.u: Wafer polishing, planarizing after copper wiring

terms.d: A thin film of silicon dioxide (SiO2) grown on the silicon surface.
terms.e: A thin protective film that doesn't conduct electricity. It forms naturally when silicon reacts with oxygen.
terms.u: Gate dielectric, isolation between devices, masking

terms.d: Growing oxide with oxygen is dry oxidation; with steam, it's wet oxidation.
terms.e: Dry is slow but dense; wet is fast but less dense. Thin, critical films use dry; thick films use wet.

terms.d: The very thin insulating film under a transistor's gate electrode.
terms.e: A thin partition that passes the gate voltage through to the channel while blocking current.
terms.u: Transistor fabrication, the switch to high-k materials

terms.d: Heat treatment that heals damage or moves atoms into stable positions by heating the wafer.
terms.e: RTP heats quickly over a short time, keeping atoms from spreading more than needed.
terms.u: Repairing the crystal after ion implantation, activating dopants

terms.d: A light-sensitive material whose properties change when exposed to light.
terms.e: Like the light-sensitive coating on photo film, only the areas hit by light change, carving in the circuit shape.
terms.u: Coated on the wafer surface, then exposed and developed

terms.d: The step that uses light to transfer the circuit pattern on a mask onto the photoresist on the wafer.
terms.e: Like using a stamp, it transfers the circuit shape with light.

terms.d: A glass plate (mask) bearing the circuit pattern to be transferred onto the wafer.
terms.e: The equivalent of a photo negative or the face of a stamp.

terms.d: How fine a line can be drawn sharply.
terms.e: The higher the resolution, the finer the circuits you can draw. Shorter wavelengths help.
terms.u: Exposure tool performance, why EUV was adopted

terms.d: The height range that can be considered in focus.
terms.e: The narrower it is, the more even slight bumps on the wafer surface blur the lines. That's why CMP is used to flatten it.

terms.d: Lithography using extreme ultraviolet light with a 13.5 nm wavelength.
terms.e: The shorter the wavelength, the finer the lines you can draw. Its wavelength is far shorter than conventional lithography's.

terms.d: A technique that pre-calculates how light bends and spreads and deliberately adjusts the mask shapes to compensate.
terms.e: Knowing corners will blur when printed, you draw them pre-corrected in the opposite direction.

terms.d: Splitting a pattern too dense to print in one go into several passes that are overlaid.
terms.e: Drawing lines too tightly packed for one pass in two or three passes. The downside is more process steps and cost.
terms.u: Fine processes before EUV, supplementing some EUV layers

terms.d: The process that carves away unwanted material following the shape drawn in photolithography.
terms.e: Like carving out a drawing with a chisel. Photolithography draws the shape; etching carves it out.
terms.u: Forming circuit patterns, cutting deep holes (vias, channel holes)

terms.d: A state created by energizing a gas into a mix of ions, electrons and radicals.
terms.e: Like the inside of a fluorescent lamp or a lightning bolt — gas that's electrically charged and glowing. It powers etching and deposition.

terms.d: The ratio of etch rates between the film you want removed and the film you want kept.
terms.e: The higher it is, the more you can carve only the needed film while protecting the one you keep.

terms.d: Anisotropic etching carves only vertically; isotropic etching carves in every direction.
terms.e: Standing circuits up straight needs anisotropic etching; isotropic etching, which spreads sideways too, is mainly used for cleaning and removal.

terms.d: An atom or molecule with an unpaired electron, which reacts very easily with other substances.
terms.e: A high-energy particle that drives chemical reactions.

terms.d: A hole's or pillar's depth (height) divided by its width.
terms.e: The higher it is, the deeper and narrower the hole. The narrower and deeper, the harder it is to dig and to fill.

terms.d: When etching a deep hole, the sidewalls bulge outward.
terms.e: The deeper you dig, the more ions spread sideways, so the middle of the hole swells like a barrel.

terms.d: The process of coating a thin film onto the wafer.
terms.e: Like painting on a thin coat, it applies the desired material to the wafer.
terms.u: Forming insulating, metal and semiconductor films

terms.d: A method that knocks material loose by physical force and coats it onto the wafer.
terms.e: Sputtering is the classic example: ions strike the material, and the atoms knocked loose stick to the wafer.

terms.d: A method where gas precursors react chemically on the wafer surface to build up a film.
terms.e: Gases react on the surface and solidify into a film. Its advantage is fast deposition.
terms.u: Forming insulating films and polysilicon films

terms.d: A method that builds films one atomic layer at a time in alternating steps, for precise thickness control.
terms.e: Slow, but it can coat very thin, uniform films all the way inside deep holes.
terms.u: High-k dielectrics, thin films in 3D structures

terms.d: How evenly a film covers raised and recessed parts of a surface.
terms.e: It checks whether bumpy floors and the insides of walls get coated to the same thickness.
terms.u: Deposition quality in deep holes and 3D structures

terms.d: The doping process that accelerates ions and drives them into the wafer.
terms.e: Ion energy and dose precisely set the depth and concentration. After implantation, annealing repairs the damage.

terms.d: The metal lines inside a chip that link devices and carry electrical signals.
terms.e: The road network linking devices, stacked in many layers.

terms.d: A small metal-filled hole that connects wiring on upper and lower layers.
terms.e: Like an elevator in a building, a passage up and down between floors.
terms.u: Multilayer wiring; a TSV is the same idea scaled up to the chip level

terms.d: A method of making wiring by first etching trenches in the insulator, filling them with copper, then polishing it back with CMP.
terms.e: Copper is hard to etch, so trenches are dug first and then filled.

terms.d: A thin metal film that keeps copper from spreading into the insulator.
terms.e: If copper spreads into the neighboring insulator, devices fail, so it's wrapped in a thin metal wall.
terms.u: The bottom and sides of copper wiring

terms.d: When a large current flows for a long time, metal atoms are pushed along by the electron flow and the wire breaks.
terms.e: Keep running a strong current through a thin wire and the path slowly wears away until it breaks.

terms.d: Signal delay caused by wiring resistance (R) and capacitance (C).
terms.e: It worsens as wires get thinner and denser, limiting the speed of high-performance chips.

terms.d: The process that electrically tests each chip on the wafer and sorts good from bad.
terms.e: It screens out bad chips before packaging, cutting wasted cost.
terms.u: End of wafer fabrication, before packaging begins

terms.d: The share of chips made that actually work properly.
terms.e: The higher the yield, the more profit from the same wafer.
terms.u: Process control, calculating cost and profit

terms.d: A test that deliberately applies stress with high heat and voltage to weed out chips that would fail early.
terms.e: A test that picks out weak chips before shipment.

terms.d: Building spare circuits ahead of time and swapping failing cells for spares to save the chip.
terms.e: Memory chips are large with many cells, so this keeps one or two bad cells from scrapping the whole chip.

terms.d: Connecting the chip to the substrate with fine metal wires.
terms.e: The oldest connection method. Cheap, but the long wires hurt speed.

terms.d: Flipping the chip over and attaching it directly to the substrate with bumps.
terms.e: Short connections make it fast, and the whole chip surface can be used for connections.

terms.d: A small metal protrusion (solder ball) that electrically connects the chip and substrate.
terms.e: A tiny contact on the underside of the chip.

terms.d: Resin that fills the gap between the chip and substrate to protect the joints.
terms.e: Filling the space between bumps with resin keeps bumps from breaking under thermal deformation.

terms.d: The process of encasing the chip in resin (EMC) to protect it from moisture and impact.
terms.e: The step that wraps the chip in a hard plastic case.

terms.d: How much a material expands as temperature rises.
terms.e: If materials expand by different amounts, heat can warp or break the joints.
terms.u: Choosing chip, substrate and underfill materials

terms.d: How well heat travels through a material.
terms.e: The higher it is, the more easily heat escapes. When a chip gets hot, performance drops.

terms.d: A semiconductor switch that turns current on and off with an electrical signal.
terms.e: A single chip holds billions of them. It's the smallest unit that makes 0s and 1s.

terms.d: The most common transistor, which uses gate voltage to switch current between source and drain.
terms.e: Like a faucet, turning the gate voltage controls the current flowing through the channel.

terms.d: The electrode in a transistor that uses voltage to decide whether current flows.
terms.e: It works like the handle of a switch.

terms.d: The path current flows through inside a transistor.
terms.e: The gate voltage opens and closes this path. FinFET and GAA change the channel's shape to improve control.

terms.d: The two ends of the channel: charge enters at the source and exits at the drain.
terms.e: They're made by doping with ion implantation.

terms.d: The minimum gate voltage at which a transistor starts to turn on.
terms.e: The gate must go above this voltage for the channel to open and current to flow.

terms.d: The gate voltage needed to change current tenfold in the turn-off region (mV/dec).
terms.e: The smaller it is, the more sharply the switch turns on and off. At room temperature, about 60 mV/dec is the limit.
terms.u: Evaluating leakage current and power efficiency

terms.d: Current that leaks unintentionally through a device that's supposed to be off.
terms.e: Like water dripping from a closed faucet. It causes power drain and heat.

terms.d: Problems that arise as the channel shortens and the gate can no longer control current properly.
terms.e: As the channel shortens, the drain's influence grows and the switch won't turn off cleanly. This is the main reason FinFET and GAA were introduced.

terms.d: As drain voltage rises, the effective channel length shortens and current creeps up.
terms.e: It's why current isn't perfectly constant even in saturation.

terms.d: If data disappears when power is off, it's volatile; if it remains, it's non-volatile.
terms.e: DRAM and SRAM are volatile; NAND flash is non-volatile.

terms.d: Memory that stores 0s and 1s as charge on a capacitor.
terms.e: The charge slowly leaks, so it must be refilled periodically. It's used as a computer's working memory.
terms.u: Main memory in servers, PCs and smartphones

terms.d: Fast memory that stores data in cells built from several transistors.
terms.e: It needs no refresh and is fast, but its large cells make capacity hard to scale.

terms.d: Non-volatile memory that keeps data even with the power off.
terms.e: It remembers information by trapping charge. It's cheap and high-capacity.

terms.d: A component that stores charge.
terms.e: In DRAM, whether charge is present or not distinguishes 0 from 1.

terms.d: Periodically reading and refilling charge that leaks away.
terms.e: Like topping up a leaky container with water over and over.

terms.d: NAND flash that increases capacity by stacking cells upward.
terms.e: Since shrinking further on a flat plane is hard, it builds upward — like a high-rise apartment instead of a house.

terms.d: A structure where the channel stands up like a fish fin and the gate wraps three sides.
terms.e: The gate wraps more sides than a flat channel, improving current control.

terms.d: A structure where the gate wraps the channel on all sides.
terms.e: One step beyond FinFET: the channel becomes thin sheets (nanosheets) wrapped on every side.

terms.d: A technology that combines a high-dielectric-constant insulator with a metal gate to reduce leakage.
terms.e: When oxide got too thin, current leaked, so a thicker insulator delivering the same effect was needed.

terms.d: A technology that moves power lines to the back of the wafer.
terms.e: To avoid signal and power lines tangling on one side, the front carries signals and the back carries power.

terms.d: A structure that stacks n-type and p-type transistors on top of each other.
terms.e: A way to save area by stacking two transistors that used to sit side by side.
terms.u: A next-gen device candidate after GAA

terms.d: High-bandwidth memory that stacks DRAM chips in many layers and connects them through a wide pathway.
terms.e: Instead of several narrow roads, it builds a wide highway. Widely used in AI accelerators.

terms.d: A passage drilled vertically through a silicon chip and filled with metal.
terms.e: Like an elevator running through a building, it lets stacked chips exchange signals.

terms.d: An intermediate substrate that holds several chips side by side and links them.
terms.e: It connects chips with short, dense wiring.

terms.d: A bonding method that joins copper pads directly, without bumps.
terms.e: It allows much tighter contact spacing and shorter connections.

terms.d: Splitting a large chip into several small chips made separately and combined in the package.
terms.e: Like Lego blocks, each function is made separately and assembled. The yield burden is smaller than making one huge chip.

terms.d: A material with properties between a conductor, which conducts electricity, and an insulator, which doesn't.
terms.e: How well it conducts can be controlled by doping, temperature, light and voltage, which is why it's used to make switches and memory.
terms.u: The chips in every electronic device

terms.d: A circuit made by placing many devices, such as transistors, on a single piece of substrate.
terms.e: This is what we usually call a "chip."
terms.u: Every semiconductor product: memory, CPUs, mobile chips and more

terms.d: A die is one piece cut from a wafer; "chip" usually means the same thing or the finished, packaged product.
terms.e: On the fab floor, one chip on the wafer is often called a die.

terms.d: A semiconductor manufacturing plant where circuits are built onto wafers.
terms.e: Hundreds of process steps happen inside. Companies operate multiple fabs, each with its own name.
terms.u: Manufacturing in general, investment and expansion news

terms.d: A workspace where dust and contaminant particles are kept to an absolute minimum.
terms.e: Circuit lines are far thinner than a hair, so a single speck of dust can cause a defect.
terms.u: Inside the fab, wearing cleanroom suits

terms.d: Fabless companies only design; foundries manufacture other companies' designs under contract; IDMs do everything from design to production themselves.
terms.e: A foundry is a manufacturing specialist that builds chips designed by others.

terms.d: Unlike memory chips, which store information, these chips handle computation, control and processing.
terms.e: CPUs, mobile application processors, image sensors and communication chips belong here. Also called non-memory semiconductors.

terms.d: A CPU is the brain that processes varied instructions in order; a GPU processes huge numbers of simple calculations at once.
terms.e: GPUs are widely used not just for graphics but also for AI training and inference.

terms.d: The empirical observation that the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every two years.
terms.e: Many say it no longer holds as fast as before because scaling has gotten harder. Advanced packaging is drawing attention to make up for it.
terms.u: Background on scaling, a common interview question

terms.d: The name for a generation of fine process technology, like 7nm, 5nm or 3nm.
terms.e: A smaller number means a newer generation, but today it no longer literally reflects actual circuit dimensions.

terms.d: Doping that adds electrons makes n-type; doping that adds holes makes p-type.
terms.e: Adding group-V elements like phosphorus or arsenic makes n-type; group-III elements like boron make p-type.

terms.d: The conduction band is the energy range where electrons move freely; the valence band is the energy range filled with electrons.
terms.e: The empty gap between them is the band gap. When electrons rise into the conduction band, they create current.
terms.u: Energy band diagrams, explaining semiconductor physics

terms.d: A region near a junction with almost no carriers.
terms.e: It forms when p-type and n-type meet and electrons and holes near the boundary find each other and disappear.
terms.u: PN junctions, MOS capacitors, around source/drain

terms.d: A device that lets current flow easily in only one direction.
terms.e: The most basic PN junction device.
terms.u: Rectification, protection circuits, LEDs and solar cells

terms.d: Applying + voltage to the p side drives current easily (forward); the opposite barely passes any (reverse).
terms.e: Forward bias lowers the barrier; reverse bias raises it and widens the depletion region.

terms.d: How well an insulator holds charge in an electric field.
terms.e: An insulator with high permittivity can gather more charge at the same thickness. Silicon dioxide's is about 3.9.
terms.u: High-k dielectrics, low-k wiring dielectrics, capacitors

terms.d: When an electron and a hole meet and disappear together, releasing energy.
terms.e: When that energy comes out as light, you get an LED.
terms.u: Depletion region formation, LEDs, analyzing device operation

terms.d: The most common semiconductor material, obtained from silicon, the main component of sand.
terms.e: A stable oxide forms easily on its surface, which makes it ideal for building transistors.

terms.d: The process of washing particles, organics and metal contamination off the wafer surface.
terms.e: It's repeated between every process step. A single speck of dust or metal ion can cause a defect.
terms.u: Wafer manufacturing, before and after every process

terms.d: A model describing how oxide thickens over time.
terms.e: At first, the reaction rate sets the thickness; as the film thickens, the rate at which oxygen penetrates the film takes over.
terms.u: Predicting film thickness from oxidation time and temperature

terms.d: A method of electrically isolating transistors by etching shallow trenches between them and filling them with insulator.
terms.e: A partition that keeps neighboring devices from leaking current into or interfering with each other.

terms.d: The overall technology of transferring circuit shapes onto the wafer with light.
terms.e: Nearly the same as "photolithography." It's the core technology driving chip scaling.

terms.d: Spinning the wafer quickly so centrifugal force spreads photoresist evenly.
terms.e: Similar to swirling pancake batter in a pan to spread it thin.

terms.d: The step after exposure that washes away the light-reacted areas with a solution to reveal the pattern.
terms.e: Like the image emerging when a photo is developed.
terms.u: The step after exposure in photolithography

terms.d: With positive photoresist, exposed areas dissolve away; with negative, exposed areas remain.
terms.e: Depending on which part remains, the mask shape is reversed.

terms.d: How wide an angle a lens can gather light from.
terms.e: A larger NA improves resolution but narrows depth of focus.

terms.d: The pattern line width most closely controlled in a process.
terms.e: Managing how far line width strays from target is at the heart of process control.
terms.u: Measuring line width after lithography and etching

terms.d: Alignment accuracy — how precisely patterns on upper and lower layers line up.
terms.e: Each layer is printed separately, so even a slight misalignment can make a via miss its wire.

terms.d: An exposure tool that moves the reticle and wafer together while shining light to transfer the pattern.
terms.e: A stepper is the older type that prints one field at a time; a scanner sweeps across as it prints and is the mainstream today.

terms.d: Etching that dissolves films by immersing them in a chemical solution.
terms.e: Relatively simple with good selectivity, but it carves sideways too (isotropic), which is bad for fine patterns.
terms.u: Cleaning, removing films on large patterns

terms.d: Etching that carves material with plasma and gases.
terms.e: It can carve straight down (anisotropic), so it's used for fine patterns.

terms.d: A dry etching method that combines chemical reactions with ion bombardment.
terms.e: The chemical reaction provides selectivity; ion bombardment provides verticality.

terms.d: A tough film added beneath the photoresist when photoresist alone can't hold up.
terms.e: It keeps the photoresist from wearing away first during deep etching.

terms.d: The thickness removed per unit of time.
terms.e: The basis for setting how long it takes to reach the target depth.

terms.d: When the sidewall beneath the mask gets carved in.
terms.e: It mostly happens in isotropic etching and makes patterns narrower than designed.

terms.d: A very thin film, from a few nanometers to a few micrometers thick.
terms.e: Chips are built by stacking dozens of these thin films.

terms.d: A PVD method where ions strike a material (target) and the atoms knocked loose stick to the wafer.
terms.e: Like one billiard ball striking another and sending it flying.

terms.d: CVD that uses plasma to deposit films at low temperature.
terms.e: Deposition happens at low temperature so structures already built aren't damaged by high heat.

terms.d: The chemical that serves as a film's raw material during deposition.
terms.e: The material that reacts to become the film — especially important in ALD and CVD.
terms.u: Choosing materials for ALD and CVD

terms.d: Silicon made of many small crystals (polycrystalline).
terms.e: It was widely used for transistor gate electrodes in the past and has largely been replaced by metal gates.

terms.d: The amount of ions implanted per unit area in ion implantation.
terms.e: The higher the dose, the higher the doping concentration.

terms.d: FEOL is the front-end stage that builds transistors; BEOL is the back-end stage that builds wiring on top.
terms.e: If you're building a house, FEOL is the rooms and fixtures, and BEOL is laying the hallways and plumbing.
terms.u: Dividing the process flow, explaining backside power (BSPDN)

terms.d: The vertical connection linking a transistor's source, drain and gate to the first wiring layer.
terms.e: The first passage between a transistor and the wiring.

terms.d: An insulating film with a low dielectric constant.
terms.e: Placed between wires, it lowers capacitance and reduces RC delay.

terms.d: A compound formed by reacting silicon with metal, used to lower contact resistance.
terms.e: Coated on the source/drain silicon so it connects well to metal contacts.

terms.d: Resistance and capacitance that weren't designed in but arise unavoidably from wiring and structure.
terms.e: They slow signals and increase power use. Their impact grows with scaling.

terms.d: A test fixture with fine needles that touch the pads of chips on the wafer.
terms.e: The needles contact the chip, send electrical signals and read the response.

terms.d: A map showing good and bad chips on a wafer by color.
terms.e: Failures clustered at the edge or on one side are clues pointing to a process problem.

terms.d: Opening up a failed chip to find the cause.
terms.e: Microscopy, cross-sectioning and other methods reveal which process step went wrong.

terms.d: A test that checks whether a product can last long under harsh conditions of temperature, humidity, voltage and so on.
terms.e: Burn-in weeds out early failures; reliability tests confirm lifetime.

terms.d: Grinding the back of the wafer to thin it.
terms.e: Thinner wafers shed heat better and make thinner packages, and it's essential for stacked packages.
terms.u: Early packaging, TSV and HBM stacking

terms.d: Cutting the wafer into individual chips.
terms.e: A saw or laser cuts along the empty lines between chips (scribe lines).

terms.d: Attaching cut chips onto a substrate or lead frame.
terms.e: Adhesive or film fixes the chip in place.

terms.d: A metal skeleton that holds the chip and connects it to external terminals.
terms.e: Both the platform the chip sits on and the legs reaching outside.

terms.d: A connection method with small solder balls arranged in a grid on the package's underside.
terms.e: Using the whole underside as contacts instead of legs greatly increases the pin count.

terms.d: A thin board that carries signals and power between the chip and the motherboard.
terms.e: The bridge connecting the chip's tiny contacts to the motherboard's large ones.

terms.d: WLP packages chips while still in wafer form; fan-out spreads wiring beyond the chip's edge to make contacts.
terms.e: It can be made thin and light without a substrate.

terms.d: A circuit style that pairs NMOS and PMOS transistors.
terms.e: When one turns on the other turns off, so almost no current flows while the value holds. That's why it's low power.

terms.d: MOSFETs where current is carried by electrons (NMOS) or holes (PMOS).
terms.e: Holes are slower than electrons, so PMOS carries less current than NMOS. Designers often make PMOS larger.

terms.d: At low drain voltage, current is proportional to voltage (linear); high enough, it becomes nearly constant (saturation).
terms.e: Like a faucet: open it more and flow increases, until at some point the pipe's width caps it.

terms.d: Ion is the current when on; Ioff is the current leaking when off.
terms.e: A good switch has a large Ion and a small Ioff. Their ratio is used to compare performance.

terms.d: In short channels, drain voltage lowers the barrier on the source side, lowering the threshold voltage.
terms.e: A classic form of short-channel effect — the drain steals some of the gate's control.

terms.d: The quantum-mechanical phenomenon of electrons passing through a thin barrier they seemingly can't cross.
terms.e: When gate oxide gets too thin, this makes leakage current rise sharply.

terms.d: A carrier that has gained a lot of energy in a strong electric field.
terms.e: When these carriers get lodged in the oxide, device characteristics gradually shift and lifetime shortens.

terms.d: Shrinking device size by a fixed ratio to pack in more and improve performance.
terms.e: Smaller means better speed and density, but short-channel effects and leakage become problems.

terms.d: Silicon deliberately stressed to deform its crystal and raise carrier mobility.
terms.e: Slightly changing the spacing between atoms lets electrons or holes run faster.

terms.d: Dynamic power is used when switching on and off; static power is used by current leaking even when off.
terms.e: With scaling, static power (leakage) has become a larger share.
terms.u: Chip power design, mobile battery life

terms.d: The smallest unit that stores one bit of information.
terms.e: A DRAM cell is one transistor and one capacitor; a NAND cell is one transistor.

terms.d: The word line selects which cell to access; the bit line reads and writes the data.
terms.e: On a grid of roads, the intersection of a horizontal and vertical line is a cell's address.
terms.u: DRAM, NAND and SRAM cell arrays

terms.d: A circuit that amplifies a tiny voltage difference on the bit line to decide 0 or 1.
terms.e: DRAM cells hold very little charge, so this amplification is essential when reading.

terms.d: NAND schemes that store 2, 3 and 4 bits per cell, respectively.
terms.e: More bits store more in the same area, but speed and endurance drop.

terms.d: The two ways flash memory traps charge.
terms.e: The charge stays trapped with the power off, so the information remains. 3D NAND mostly uses charge trap.

terms.d: In NAND, reads and writes happen per page; erases happen per block.
terms.e: Several pages make a block. So even to rewrite just part, you have to manage it block by block.

terms.d: In NAND, writing data is called programming, and deleting it is called erasing.
terms.e: Each cycle wears the oxide, so the number of cycles is limited.

terms.d: Bandwidth is the amount of data moved per second; latency is the time from request to response.
terms.e: On a road, bandwidth is the number of lanes and latency is the travel time.

terms.d: DDR is the DRAM standard for PCs and servers; LPDDR is the low-power standard for mobile.
terms.e: It sends data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock for speed. Higher generation numbers are faster.

terms.d: Small, fast memory that keeps frequently used data close to the CPU.
terms.e: Mostly made of SRAM. Like keeping only the books you use most on your desk.
terms.u: The memory hierarchy inside CPUs and GPUs

terms.d: Flash memory that's non-volatile with fast reads, used to store program code.
terms.e: It costs more per unit of capacity than NAND but can read any location quickly.

terms.d: Memories that store information using new principles such as magnetism, resistance or phase change.
terms.e: Research aims for memory that keeps data with the power off while running close to DRAM speeds.

terms.d: A next-gen EUV tool that raises numerical aperture (NA) from 0.33 to 0.55 to draw finer patterns.
terms.e: It uses larger optics to gather light from a wider angle. The tools are extremely expensive.

terms.d: A GAA nanosheet structure that places an insulating wall between NMOS and PMOS to tighten spacing.
terms.e: It's being researched as a device structure candidate after GAA.

terms.d: Materials with a band gap wider than silicon's, notably SiC (silicon carbide) and GaN (gallium nitride).
terms.e: They withstand high voltage and temperature, so they're used in power semiconductors like EV inverters and chargers.

terms.d: Integrating devices that send and receive data with light onto a silicon chip.
terms.e: Faster than electrical signals with less heat, it's increasingly used for data center communication.

terms.d: A chip built to process the matrix calculations AI relies on quickly and efficiently.
terms.e: GPUs also serve as AI accelerators, and smartphones include a separate NPU.

terms.d: Technology that handles part of the computation inside memory to cut the burden of moving data.
terms.e: The goal is to save the time and power spent moving data over long distances.

terms.d: An interconnect standard that links CPUs, memory and accelerators at high speed and lets memory be expanded or shared.
terms.e: It's drawing attention as a way to expand memory in servers.

terms.d: 2.5D places chips side by side on an interposer; 3D stacks chips vertically.
terms.e: 2.5D connects neighbors on the same level; 3D connects between layers. TSVs and hybrid bonding are key to 3D.

terms.d: A 2.5D packaging technology that mounts chips on an interposer and then attaches it to a substrate. It's TSMC's name for it.
terms.e: Widely used to bundle AI accelerators and HBM in one package.

terms.d: A bonding bump much smaller than a regular bump.
terms.e: Used to stack chips in HBM. The smaller and denser they get, the more connections fit.

terms.d: SoC puts many functions on one chip; SiP puts several chips in one package.
terms.e: When one chip gets too big to make easily, splitting it and combining the pieces in a package (SiP, chiplets) is on the rise.

terms.d: An open standard that unifies how chiplets connect to each other.
terms.e: The idea is that chiplets from different companies can be joined using the same specification.
